title: Jnaneshwar
hook: a yogi rides in on a tiger, and the children ride out on a wall
carry: a wall only has to be willing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jnaneshwar again: the Gita opened in Marathi, sweeter than nectar, with all the credit given to his brother. What did you explain in plain words? Day nine hundred fifteen.

Here comes a yogi, riding a tiger. In his hand, instead of a whip, a live snake. Behind him, a crowd of disciples. His name is Changdev, and tradition remembers him as a man of great yogic powers. He has heard about a young saint at Alandi, and he's coming to see him, in the way a person with powers might arrive. At the other end of the road, Jnaneshwar and his brothers and sister are sitting on a low wall in the sun. Someone runs up: he's coming. Today, the last day with Jnaneshwar, and two very different entrances.
screen: `A YOGI ON A TIGER.` → `A SNAKE FOR A WHIP.` → `CHILDREN ON A WALL.`

segments.voice: The story starts with a letter that was never written. Before setting out, Changdev wanted to send word ahead, but he couldn't decide how to address Jnaneshwar. As an equal? As a teacher? As a boy? So he sent a blank sheet. Muktabai, the sister, is said to have read it and remarked that all his years of practice had left him blank. Then the tiger, the snake, the crowd. Jnaneshwar doesn't climb down. The story says he asks the wall to move, and the wall carries the four children down the road to meet the yogi. Changdev, who had mastered a living tiger, sees children riding on stone, and the pride goes out of him. Tradition says he became a disciple, some tellings say of Muktabai herself. Notice what the wall is. It isn't a show of force. A tiger has to be tamed. A wall just has to be willing. That's the joke at the heart of the story, and it isn't only on Changdev; it's on anyone who thinks arriving has to be impressive. Then hold that next to how Jnaneshwar ends his book. At the close of the Jnaneshwari he asks God for a gift, a pasayadan, and the gift isn't for himself. He asks that the crookedness of the wicked fall away, that they come to love doing good, and that all beings become friends to one another. Tradition says that later, at Alandi, still a young man, Jnaneshwar entered samadhi, a final meditation, and that his shrine there is honored as the place where he still sits. A boy who once went begging for a letter, and later received a blank one, ended by asking for the whole world's good.
screen: `A BLANK LETTER.` · `THE WALL THAT MOVES.` · `A TIGER TAMED, A WALL WILLING.` · `THE PASAYADAN: A GIFT FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit as you are, the way the children sat on the wall: no special posture, no effort to look like anything. Let the breath come. Notice any part of you that wants to arrive impressively today, in a meeting, a message, a room. Let it soften, the way a wall is simply willing. Then, for the rest of the sit, wish good for people you'll see today, including one who has been hard on you. If you pray, you can ask good for them in words you already use. The bell holds the time.
Jnaneshwar. The Marathi saint who rode a willing wall to meet a yogi on a tiger, and closed his book asking good for all beings.
Your line: a wall only has to be willing. Today, skip the impressive entrance once. Show up plainly, and wish the room well. Day nine hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Marathi-speaking devotees often recite the Pasayadan at the close of worship or gatherings, and pilgrims visit Jnaneshwar's samadhi shrine at Alandi, where his palanquin sets out on the Varkari pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

ask the wall to carry you.
send him a blank letter of your own.

original.note: Marathi, in Devanagari: the gift Jnaneshwar asks of God at the end of his book.

trapdoor: what you thought: a contest of miracles, tiger against wall.
what it means: power needs a tamed tiger; a wall only needs to be willing, and the yogi's pride falls away.
what a scholar hears: the Jnaneshwari closes with the Pasayadan, a prayer for the good of all beings rather than the saint's own.

notes: Editor pass: removed 'all of us who think' (told listeners what they believe); howItsDone no longer implies the whole Varkari pilgrimage begins at Alandi.
Audit: 'not long after' the book removed (an implied interval the sources don't give here); samadhi now placed only 'later, still a young man'.
All paraphrase. The Pasayadan is described, not quoted or newly written; confirm the paraphrase (crookedness of the wicked falling away, love of good deeds, friendship among beings).
Changdev's age (tradition gives a very long life) and Jnaneshwar's age at samadhi are deliberately omitted under the claims rule.
Muktabai's remark on the blank letter and Changdev becoming her disciple are given as 'is said to' / 'some tellings'; confirm.
Samadhi described as 'a final meditation' and the shrine 'honored as the place where he still sits'; a Keeper should confirm the wording of sanjivan samadhi.
